chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majilawayh narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn, from Mu'adh ibn Muslim, the seller of al-Harawi, who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when they mentioned illness. He said: 'Treat your illnesses with charity (Sadaqah). And it is not difficult for any one of you to give charity with the food of his day. Indeed, the Angel of Death is presented with the decree to take the soul of the servant; if he gives charity, it is said to him: 'Return the decree to him.'

key_terms.الصَّدَقَهِ: Charity (Sadaqah), voluntary alms given for spiritual and physical benefit
key_terms.الصَّکُّ: The decree or document, specifically the decree of death
key_terms.قَبْضِ رُوحِ الْعَبْدِ: Taking the soul of the servant
key_terms.قُوتِ یَوْمِهِ: Food of his day, referring to a day's sustenance

ai.seo_question: How does charity (Sadaqah) affect illness and death according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) prescribes charity as a spiritual remedy for illness, highlighting the metaphysical mechanism where the Angel of Death receives the decree of death (as-Sakk) and may be commanded to return the soul if the deceased has given charity. This narration underscores the tangible efficacy of even modest charity, such as one day's sustenance, in altering divine decree and delaying death, a concept deeply rooted in Shia eschatological traditions regarding the intercession of good deeds.
